title: See your money clearly: needs, wants, income and leaks

say: See your money clearly: needs, wants, income and leaks.
This is the video for Module 1, Understanding Money and Your Financial Life.
Financial literacy simply means understanding money well enough to make good choices with it. A market woman who knows what each bag of rice cost her is practising it every day.
Almost every money choice falls into one of five decisions. Earn is how money comes in.

say: A need keeps you safe, healthy and earning. A want makes life nicer but can wait.
Question one. What happens if I do not buy this today? If my family goes hungry, falls sick, loses shelter or I cannot work, it is a need.

panel.heading: Need or want?
items: What happens if I do not buy it today?

say: Question two. Is there a cheaper version that meets the same need? Food is a need, but eating out every day is partly a want. The basic version is the need. The extra cost is the want.

panel.heading: Need or want?
items: What happens if I do not buy it today?

say: Question three. Can it wait 30 days? Then write it on a wants list instead of buying it now. Many items drop off the list on their own.
Wants are not bad. A small planned treat is better than a big unplanned one that leaves you short for rent.

panel.heading: Need or want?
items: What happens if I do not buy it today?
panel.rule: Pay for needs first, save next, then enjoy wants.

say: For example, Aisha, a hairdresser in Kaduna, wrote down everything she spent in one week. Foodstuff, bus fare and hair products for clients were needs.
But suya and soft drinks on three evenings cost about 7,500 naira. And a contribution for a friend's aso ebi was about 15,000 naira.
Out of about 58,500 naira, about 22,500 was clearly wants.
She did not cut every want. She kept one suya evening and declined the aso ebi this time. That freed about 20,000 naira for her emergency savings.
Plan with take-home money. For a business, that is profit, not total sales. When income changes month to month, plan with a careful average, not your best month.
For example, Funke runs a small food canteen in Ibadan. Her profit over six months was about 560,000 naira.

panel.heading: Funke finds a safe monthly figure
items: Six months of profit: about 560,000 naira
Extra in good months goes to savings

say: That is an average of about 93,000 naira a month.

panel.heading: Funke finds a safe monthly figure
items: Six months of profit: about 560,000 naira
Extra in good months goes to savings

say: Her lowest month was about 70,000.

panel.heading: Funke finds a safe monthly figure
items: Six months of profit: about 560,000 naira
Extra in good months goes to savings

say: So she plans her home spending on 80,000 naira, between the lowest month and the average. In any month she makes more, the extra goes into a separate savings account. In a weak month, that buffer fills the gap.

say: Most people know their big expenses but are surprised by the small ones. The only way to know is to track. Choose your tool.

panel.heading: Track for 30 days
items: Choose a notebook, phone note or Google Sheets
Write date, item and amount every time
Add up and compare at month end

say: Every time you spend, write the date, what you bought, and the amount. Do it immediately, or at the end of each day at the latest.

panel.heading: Track for 30 days
items: Choose a notebook, phone note or Google Sheets
Write date, item and amount every time
Add up and compare at month end

say: Include every channel: cash, transfers, POS, airtime and data, and money given to others.

panel.heading: Track for 30 days
items: Choose a notebook, phone note or Google Sheets
Write date, item and amount every time
Add up and compare at month end

say: Each week, group the spending into categories like food, transport and children. At month end, add each category and compare it with what you expected. The point is information, not guilt.

say: For example, Blessing, a teacher in Port Harcourt, tracked one month. She spent about 800 naira a day on drinks and snacks at work. Over 22 working days, that is about 17,600 naira a month.

cards.d: About 800 naira a day on drinks and snacks. Over 22 working days, about 17,600 naira a month.
Annual rent of about 480,000 naira means setting aside about 40,000 naira every month.
School fees of 270,000 naira a year means about 22,500 naira a month.

say: Irregular costs like annual rent feel like emergencies, though we know they are coming. The fix is to divide by 12. Her rent of about 480,000 naira means about 40,000 a month.

say: When you read your bank or mobile money history, look for charges you do not recognise, forgotten subscriptions, or transfers you did not make.
Report them to your bank immediately through its official app, branch or customer care line, never through a number someone sends you.

panel.heading: Check your app history
items: Look for charges you do not recognise
Report anything you did not authorise
Use only the bank's official contacts
